But the final paragraph only rewrites each mutual-edge condition as an integer-square condition; it derives no further uniform restriction and neither proves nor excludes four neighbors satisfying all six conditions. The candidate explicitly leaves that obligation, and the main sextuple existence question, unresolved. This blocks closure of the broader target; it does not invalidate the auxiliary lemma.","required_action":"Keep the result partial. To close the unresolved target, supply a proof resolving the six mutual-edge system for four distinct common neighbors, or a complete witness/obstruction for the main sextuple question; do not infer either from the individual-neighbor restrictions."}],"confirmed_fragments":[{"claim":"Every nonzero rational common neighbor of -1 and 1 has the stated parametrization.","reasoning":"Choose rational u,v with u²=1+x and v²=1−x. Then (u,v) lies on U²+V²=2 and u≠1 since x≠0. The line through (1,1) and (u,v) has finite rational slope t=(v−1)/(u−1). Its second intersection with the circle yields x=4t(1−t²)/(1+t²)². Writing t=m/n in lowest terms with n>0 gives the claimed form; nonzero x implies m≠0 and m≠±n."},{"claim":"For the primitive parameters in the claim, the reduced denominator is r², where r=(m²+n²)/gcd(m²+n²,2); r is odd, at least 5, and all its prime divisors are 1 modulo 4.","reasoning":"For odd p dividing q=m²+n², p divides neither m nor n. If p also divided n²−m², it would divide 2m², contradicting primitivity. Thus no odd prime of q cancels from the denominator q². If q is even, m,n are odd, q≡2 mod 8 and 8 divides n²−m²; hence v₂(N)≥5 while v₂(q²)=2, so exactly the denominator's factor 4 cancels. This proves the denominator formula. For every odd p dividing r, (m/n)²≡−1 mod p, so p≡1 mod 4. The restrictions on primitive nonzero m,n and the exclusion m=±n imply r≥5."},{"claim":"The reduced numerator is divisible by 24.","reasoning":"If q is odd, mn is even and 8 divides N; if q is even, 8 divides n²−m² and after cancellation by 4 the numerator remains divisible by 8. Modulo 3, either 3 divides mn or the nonzero squares m²,n² agree, so 3 divides n²−m². Also 3 cannot divide q for primitive m,n, since a sum of two squares is 0 modulo 3 only when both are 0. Reduction therefore preserves divisibility by 3 as well as by 8."},{"claim":"The mutual-edge reformulation is valid but does not resolve simultaneous feasibility.","reasoning":"For x_i=u_i/r_i², x_ix_j+1=(u_i u_j+r_i²r_j²)/(r_i r_j)². Each common neighbor lies strictly between −1 and 1, so this edge value is positive. A positive integer divided by a rational square is a rational square exactly when the integer is an integer square. This is an equivalent reformulation, not an additional restriction or a resolution of the six conditions."}] }]}}
